text: The biggest mistake travelers make before flying to Japan is packing $160 running shoes like Hokas or On Clouds. You think you bought the ultimate walking shoe, but you're setting yourself up for wrecked feet by day two.
super: The #1 footwear mistake travelers make in Japan ✈️

text: These shoes are built to move a runner forward for forty minutes, not for someone walking twenty-five thousand steps across Japan. When you are exploring Tokyo, Kyoto, or Osaka, you are not just taking a casual stroll. You are climbing five flights of subway stairs, walking miles across concrete train stations, standing on packed trains, and navigating hard pavement for eight, nine, sometimes ten hours straight. Three things people overlook until they are already thousands of miles from home.

Number one, that soft cushioning in the store does not tell you the whole story. Hokas use thick, squishy foam designed to bounce a runner forward on a flat road. But in Japan, you spend hours standing on crowded trains, waiting in line for food, and standing on museum floors. That soft foam packs completely flat under your body weight. And On Clouds use hollow pods that compress under constant pressure. Once that cushioning flattens out, your arches sink, leaving you with zero support right when your feet have miles left to walk.
super: 1. Soft foam packs flat while standing 📉

text: Number two, Hokas and On Clouds were not built for city hazards and winter weather. In Japan, you are constantly walking across polished subway tiles, metal train grates, and steep stone temple steps. And with winter here, those surfaces get wet, slick, and covered in patches of ice or snow. The massive soles on Hokas make your feet unstable, wobbling over every curb and putting strain on your knees. And the smooth, hollow pods on On Clouds offer almost no grip on slick wet floors. One slip on an icy train entrance or wet tile staircase can end your trip on day one. That is where a slip-resistant outsole matters. You need real grip, not an unstable running platform.
super: 2. Dangerous on slick tiles, ice & snow ❄️

text: Number three, the toe box is narrow, and the upper does not stretch. Both Hokas and On Clouds are built with rigid, tapered toe boxes meant to lock a runner's foot in place. But after walking twenty thousand steps on hard concrete, your feet naturally swell. When your toes get crammed together with nowhere to go, that friction leads to burning arches, blisters, and throbbing nerve pain. If your shoes feel tight by lunch, you are loosening your laces on a bench outside a shrine when you still have half your day to go.
super: 3. Narrow toe boxes crush swelling feet 🦶

text: That is why Comfortwear built the exact opposite of an athletic running shoe. They did not design it for marathon runners. They built it for people whose feet have to survive real life: nurses, healthcare workers, and travelers who want to actually enjoy the trip they spent years saving for. A roomy, wide toe box lets your toes spread out naturally so you stay balanced. A flexible stretch knit upper gives your feet breathing room as they swell throughout the day. And built-in structural arch support holds your feet firm hour after hour, paired with a slip-resistant outsole that grips slick station tiles, wet pavement, and winter slush.
